Before changing metadata such as directory entries or allocation maps, the filesystem writes the intended change to a journal; after a crash, it replays or discards journal entries to return to a consistent structure. Note that journaling protects metadata structure by default, not necessarily your file contents, which is why applications still need fsync. Kafka's findings matter because Kafka's workload, heavy sequential appends across many partitions, resembles many log-structured systems. XFS's design for parallel I/O and large files delivered lower and more consistent append latency. The Kafka docs also contain an important warning: the ext4 mount options that make ext4 fast, such as data=writeback, are unsafe on power loss. Those options relax the ordering between data and metadata writes, which can leave files pointing at garbage after a crash. The broader lesson is that filesystem tuning for speed can quietly trade away safety, so treat any performance-oriented mount option as a durability decision too.

quiz.q: Why is tuning ext4 with data=writeback to match XFS's speed a risky idea?
quiz.a: Kafka's docs warn such fast ext4 mount options are unsafe on power loss; they relax write ordering, risking corrupted data after a crash. XFS needs no such tuning.

section: 4.6 Filesystems on the node, and why databases care
title: write() isn't durable. fsync() is.
body: By default, a write() call only copies data into the kernel's page cache in memory. The kernel writes it to the disk later, at a time of its choosing. If the machine loses power before that, the data is gone even though write() returned successfully. To make data durable, an application calls fsync(), which forces the file's dirty pages and metadata to stable storage and waits until that is done. Only after fsync returns is the data safe.
deeper: The page cache exists for performance: buffering writes in memory lets the kernel combine them, reorder them and write efficiently in the background, and it lets reads of recently used data come from RAM. The cost is a gap between what the application thinks it wrote and what is actually on disk. Dirty pages, modified in memory but not yet written, are the vulnerable window. fsync closes the window for a given file by flushing its dirty data and the metadata needed to find it, then blocking until the storage confirms. This is why the chapter opens with the requirement that a write be safe once fsync returns: that promise is the foundation every database builds on. It also explains crash-consistent snapshots, which capture what is on the volume but not what is still in the page cache. And it explains the price of durability: every fsync waits for at least one full storage round trip, which ties database commit rates directly to storage latency.

quiz.q: An application's write() returned success, then power failed. Why might the data be lost?
quiz.a: write() only copied data into the kernel page cache. Without fsync forcing dirty pages to stable storage, unflushed data vanishes on power loss.

section: 4.6 Filesystems on the node, and why databases care
title: Commit rate is capped by fsync latency, hence group commit
body: A database commit is safe only after its write-ahead log record has been fsync'd, so every commit pays at least one storage round trip. With 0.5 ms network latency, a single commit stream cannot exceed about 2,000 commits per second. With local NVMe at tens of microseconds, the ceiling is much higher. This is why databases batch commits, a technique called group commit: many transactions share one fsync, so the round-trip cost is spread across them.
deeper: This is Little's Law applied to durability. If each commit must wait for an fsync of 0.5 ms before the next in the same stream can proceed, the stream completes at most 1 / 0.0005 = 2,000 commits per second, regardless of how many IOPS the volume is provisioned for. Two responses exist, mirroring the fixes for any latency-bound workload. Group commit is the parallelism route: while one fsync is in flight, other transactions queue up, and the next fsync flushes all their WAL records at once, turning many commits into one I/O. The cost is slightly higher latency per commit in exchange for much higher throughput. The other route is lower latency: local NVMe at tens of microseconds raises the ceiling by an order of magnitude, one reason latency-sensitive databases move to local disks. The key takeaways summarize it: databases live or die by fsync, and commit rate is bounded by fsync latency. It also explains why benchmarks with fsync disabled wildly overstate real commit rates.

quiz.q: With 0.5 ms storage latency, why can't a single commit stream exceed about 2,000 commits/s, and what helps?
quiz.a: Each commit waits for one WAL fsync round trip: 1/0.0005 = 2,000. Group commit shares one fsync across many transactions; lower-latency storage raises the ceiling.

section: 4.6 Filesystems on the node, and why databases care
title: PostgreSQL's 2018 fsync surprise: errors that vanish
body: In 2018 the PostgreSQL community found that on Linux, when a background write-back of dirty pages fails, the kernel can mark those pages clean and drop the data. A later fsync, possibly from another process, may not report the error at all. The data is silently lost. PostgreSQL's response was to treat any fsync failure as fatal, panicking and recovering from its write-ahead log, instead of retrying. The lesson: after an fsync error, you cannot trust the page cache.
deeper: The intuitive way to handle a failed fsync is to retry until it succeeds. The 2018 discovery showed why that is dangerous on Linux. When the kernel's background write-back fails, it may mark the affected pages clean even though they never reached disk, and discard the error. A retried fsync then succeeds, because from the kernel's view nothing is dirty, and the application believes its data is durable when it is actually gone. The error might also be reported to a different process than the one that later calls fsync. PostgreSQL relies on its local WAL and data files being truly on disk for committed transactions, so it chose the only safe action: PANIC, crash the database, and on restart replay the WAL, which rebuilds state from records known to be durable, rather than trusting whatever the page cache holds. Kernel developers pointed to direct I/O as the long-term answer, since it avoids relying on the page cache's write-back behavior. Contrast Kafka, which relies on replicas rather than local fsync for durability.

quiz.q: Why did PostgreSQL decide to crash on fsync failure rather than retry the fsync?
quiz.a: On Linux a failed write-back can mark pages clean and drop data, so a retried fsync may succeed falsely. Crashing and replaying the WAL is the only safe recovery.

section: 4.6 Filesystems on the node, and why databases care
title: Direct I/O: databases that skip the page cache entirely
body: With O_DIRECT, reads and writes bypass the kernel's page cache and go straight to the storage device. Databases that manage their own buffer pool, such as MySQL InnoDB as it is commonly configured, use direct I/O for two reasons: to avoid caching the same data twice, once in the database's buffer pool and again in the kernel, and to control exactly when writes reach the disk. Kernel developers pointed to direct I/O as the long-term answer to the fsync problem.
deeper: A database with its own buffer pool already decides which pages to keep in memory, based on knowledge the kernel lacks, such as which index pages are hot or which pages belong to an uncommitted transaction. Letting the kernel also cache those pages wastes memory on duplicates and adds another layer that decides when data is written. With O_DIRECT, the database's writes go to the device on its own schedule, so its durability logic does not depend on the page cache's write-back behavior. That is why kernel developers, discussing PostgreSQL's 2018 fsync discovery, pointed to direct I/O as the long-term answer: if data never sits in the page cache, the kernel cannot silently drop it after a failed write-back. The trade-off is responsibility: the application must do its own caching well and issue I/O efficiently, often with enough parallelism to satisfy Little's Law, since it loses the kernel's readahead and write combining. Databases without a sophisticated buffer pool generally benefit from the page cache instead.

quiz.q: Why would a database with its own buffer pool open its files with O_DIRECT?
quiz.a: To avoid caching data twice (buffer pool plus page cache) and to control exactly when writes reach disk instead of relying on kernel write-back.

section: 4.6 Filesystems on the node, and why databases care
title: Common mistake: sizing production from an fsync-off benchmark
body: A common error is benchmarking a database on a volume where a write cache is 'helping', or with fsync disabled, and then sizing production from the resulting number. Those settings skip the storage round trip that every real commit must pay, so the benchmark wildly overstates throughput. Your real commit rate is bounded by fsync latency on the real storage. Always benchmark with the exact durability settings you will run in production, or the capacity plan will fail under load.
deeper: The trap is that disabling durability makes numbers look spectacular. Without fsync, commits complete as soon as data is in memory, so the benchmark measures memory speed rather than storage speed. With fsync on, each commit stream is capped by storage latency: about 2,000 commits per second per stream at 0.5 ms network latency, before group commit. A plan sized on the inflated figure might provision a fraction of the needed servers, and the gap only appears when production traffic arrives. Write caches create a subtler version of the same problem: if a cache acknowledges writes before they are on stable storage, the benchmark is fast but may not reflect what the production storage path does, or may not be power-safe. The same principle applies to filesystem options such as ext4's data=writeback, which Kafka's documentation warns is unsafe on power loss. The rule generalizes: a performance number is only meaningful alongside the durability guarantees it was measured with, so benchmark the configuration you will actually run.

quiz.q: Why does a benchmark with fsync disabled lead to under-provisioned production databases?
quiz.a: It skips the storage round trip each real commit pays, so it measures memory speed. Real commit rate is bounded by fsync latency on the actual storage.

title: Kubernetes was built for stateless pods; data breaks that
body: Kubernetes was designed around stateless pods: if one dies, kill it and start another anywhere in the cluster. Storage breaks that model, because data lives in one place, on a particular volume or disk, and a replacement pod needs to find exactly that data again. Kubernetes solves this with a set of abstractions, PersistentVolumes, PersistentVolumeClaims, StorageClasses, CSI drivers, snapshots, StatefulSets and operators, that give stateful workloads durable disks inside a system built for disposable containers.
deeper: For stateless services, the scheduler's freedom to place a pod on any node is a feature: it enables bin packing, rolling upgrades and self-healing. Stateful workloads constrain that freedom. A database pod must be reunited with its volume, and that volume may be zonal, like an EBS volume that cannot leave its Availability Zone, or local, tied to a single node's NVMe. Moving it takes time, may be impossible across zones, or may mean data loss with local disks. The abstractions in this section each address part of the problem: claims and classes separate what an application asks for from how storage is provided; CSI drivers connect Kubernetes to real storage systems; binding modes keep volumes and pods in the same zone; StatefulSets give pods stable identities that map to stable volumes; and operators encode the database-specific operations Kubernetes knows nothing about. The section ends with the operational risks, because running databases on Kubernetes works, but its failure modes differ from stateless apps and must be designed for.

quiz.q: Why does persistent storage conflict with Kubernetes' original design model?
quiz.a: Kubernetes assumes a failed pod can be restarted anywhere. Data lives in one place, so a replacement pod must reach that specific volume, constraining scheduling.

title: PV and PVC: the storage and the request for it
body: A PersistentVolume, or PV, is a piece of storage in the cluster, such as an EBS volume, a Persistent Disk, a local disk or an NFS share. Its lifecycle is independent of any pod. A PersistentVolumeClaim, or PVC, is a user's request for storage, for example 'I need 100 GiB, ReadWriteOnce, class fast-ssd'. The Kubernetes control plane binds each PVC to one PV, one-to-one, and the pod then mounts the claim rather than the underlying storage.
deeper: The split mirrors a common pattern: separate what you need from how it is provided. Application authors write PVCs describing size, access mode and class, without knowing whether the cluster runs on AWS, Google Cloud or bare metal. Cluster administrators or automated provisioners supply PVs that satisfy those requests. The one-to-one binding means a claimed volume belongs to that claim until released, so two unrelated workloads cannot accidentally share a disk. Because a PV's lifecycle is independent of pods, a pod can die and be replaced while its claim, and therefore its data, persists; the replacement simply mounts the same PVC. What happens to the PV when the claim itself is deleted depends on the reclaim policy, Delete or Retain. The analogy used later for snapshots follows the same shape: a VolumeSnapshot is a user's request like a PVC, and a VolumeSnapshotContent is the actual snapshot like a PV. Understanding this request-versus-resource split makes the rest of Kubernetes storage much easier to follow.

quiz.q: Why does Kubernetes separate PersistentVolumeClaims from PersistentVolumes?
quiz.a: Apps request storage (size, access mode, class) without knowing the backend, while PVs represent actual storage. Binding one-to-one lets data outlive pods and keeps apps portable.

title: StorageClass and dynamic provisioning: volumes on demand
body: A StorageClass describes a kind of storage, which provisioner creates it, and with what parameters, for example EBS gp3 with 6,000 IOPS. With dynamic provisioning, when a PVC names a StorageClass and no existing PV matches, the provisioner creates a brand-new volume on demand. No administrator has to pre-create disks. An example class named db-gp3 uses provisioner ebs.csi.aws.com with type gp3, 6,000 IOPS, 500 MiB/s throughput, reclaimPolicy Retain, WaitForFirstConsumer binding and volume expansion allowed.
deeper: Without dynamic provisioning, administrators would have to guess ahead of time how many volumes of which sizes to create, and users would wait for them. StorageClasses make storage self-service: a team writes a PVC referencing a class, and the provisioner calls the cloud API to create a volume matching the class's parameters. The db-gp3 example encodes several good production choices in one object. Parameters set the EBS type and provision IOPS and throughput separately, taking advantage of gp3's independent performance knobs. reclaimPolicy: Retain keeps the cloud volume when the claim is deleted, protecting against accidental data loss. volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer delays creating the volume until a pod is scheduled, so a zonal EBS volume lands in the pod's zone. allowVolumeExpansion: true lets claims grow later, using the elastic capacity of network volumes. A cluster typically offers several classes, for example a cheap general class and a high-performance database class, and each PVC chooses one by name.

quiz.q: What does dynamic provisioning do when a PVC names a StorageClass and no PV matches?
quiz.a: The StorageClass's provisioner creates a new volume on demand with the class's parameters, so no one has to pre-create disks.

title: Access modes: one node, many readers, many writers, or one pod
body: Kubernetes volumes declare access modes. ReadWriteOnce means the volume can be mounted read-write by one node. ReadOnlyMany means many nodes can mount it read-only. ReadWriteMany means many nodes can mount it read-write, which usually requires a shared filesystem. ReadWriteOncePod restricts read-write access to exactly one pod. The mode must match what the underlying storage can do: a typical cloud block volume supports ReadWriteOnce, while ReadWriteMany normally needs a network filesystem.
deeper: Access modes reflect the nature of the storage underneath. A block device has no locking or coordination between writers, so two machines writing the same block volume independently would corrupt each other's filesystem. That is why block volumes such as EBS are typically ReadWriteOnce. ReadWriteMany workloads, such as shared content directories used by many pods, are usually backed by managed network filesystems like Amazon EFS, Google Filestore or Azure Files, which implement POSIX semantics across many clients. ReadWriteOncePod is stricter than ReadWriteOnce. ReadWriteOnce is per node, so two pods on the same node could both mount the volume; ReadWriteOncePod guarantees only one pod can, which is valuable for databases that must never have two instances writing the same data files. ReadOnlyMany suits distributing static data, such as reference datasets, to many nodes. Choosing the right mode is a correctness decision, not just a capability check: pick the most restrictive mode your workload allows.

quiz.q: Why is ReadWriteOncePod safer than ReadWriteOnce for a database volume?
quiz.a: ReadWriteOnce limits access to one node, so two pods on that node could both write. ReadWriteOncePod guarantees only a single pod can mount it read-write.

title: Reclaim policy: Retain is the safer default for databases
body: A PersistentVolume's reclaim policy decides what happens to the underlying storage when its claim is deleted. With Delete, the cloud volume is removed along with the PVC. With Retain, the volume is kept for manual cleanup, so the data still exists even after the claim is gone. For production databases, Retain is often the safer choice, because a mistaken deletion of a claim, or of a whole namespace, would otherwise destroy the data permanently.
deeper: Delete is convenient for ephemeral environments: test clusters and preview deployments clean up after themselves automatically, and nobody pays for orphaned disks. But in production, convenience cuts the wrong way. The chapter's list of operational risks includes accidental deletion: a kubectl delete namespace can remove every PVC in that namespace, and with a Delete reclaim policy the cloud volumes go too, taking the database with them. Retain breaks that chain: Kubernetes objects can be deleted and recreated, but the volume, and the data, stays until a human deliberately removes it. The cost is housekeeping, since retained volumes must be tracked and cleaned up manually or they accumulate charges. Retain is one layer of defense, not the whole plan. The chapter recommends combining it with deletion protection and off-cluster backups, since snapshots and volumes inside the same account or cluster can still be lost to broader mistakes. The example db-gp3 StorageClass sets reclaimPolicy: Retain for exactly this reason.

quiz.q: What happens to a database's data after 'kubectl delete namespace' under Delete vs Retain reclaim policies?
quiz.a: With Delete, PVCs are removed and their cloud volumes deleted, destroying data. With Retain, the volumes remain for manual recovery or cleanup.

title: WaitForFirstConsumer: keep the volume in the pod's zone
body: The volumeBindingMode setting WaitForFirstConsumer delays creating a volume until a pod that uses it has been scheduled, so the volume is created in the same zone as that pod. Without it, using Immediate binding, a zonal EBS volume might be created in zone A while the scheduler later places the pod in zone B. Because the volume cannot attach across zones, the pod can never start and stays stuck in a pending state.
deeper: The root cause is ordering. With Immediate binding, the provisioner creates the volume as soon as the PVC appears, choosing a zone before the scheduler has considered the pod's constraints, such as available CPU, memory, node affinity or anti-affinity with other replicas. Since zonal block volumes, like EBS, cannot move to another Availability Zone, any mismatch is permanent for that pod: the scheduler cannot place it where the volume lives if that zone lacks capacity, and it cannot use the volume anywhere else. WaitForFirstConsumer reverses the order: schedule the pod first, taking all constraints into account, then create the volume in the chosen zone. The Kubernetes docs also recommend WaitForFirstConsumer for local persistent volumes, where the same reasoning applies at node level instead of zone level. The key takeaways sum it up: WaitForFirstConsumer keeps volumes in the right zone. It is a small setting with an outsized effect on whether stateful pods start reliably.

quiz.q: What goes wrong if a StorageClass for zonal EBS volumes uses Immediate binding?
quiz.a: The volume may be created in one zone before the pod is scheduled. If the pod lands in another zone, it cannot attach the volume and stays pending.

title: CSI drivers: how Kubernetes actually talks to storage
body: The Container Storage Interface, CSI, is a standard API between container orchestrators and storage systems. Before CSI, storage plugins were compiled into Kubernetes itself. Now each vendor ships a CSI driver, such as the EBS CSI driver, the GCE PD driver or Ceph's driver, that runs as pods in the cluster. A driver has a controller part, which creates, deletes, attaches and snapshots volumes through the cloud API, and a node part, which formats and mounts the device on the host.
deeper: Moving storage plugins out of the Kubernetes codebase decoupled vendors from Kubernetes release cycles: a storage provider can fix bugs or add features by shipping a new driver, without waiting for a Kubernetes release. The full provisioning flow shows how the pieces fit. A PVC requests 100Gi of class db-gp3. The StorageClass names the EBS CSI provisioner. With WaitForFirstConsumer, the pod is scheduled onto a node first; then the CSI controller calls the cloud API to create a new EBS volume in the pod's zone. The resulting PV is bound to the PVC. The device is attached to the chosen node (an attach call through the cloud API, which the text assigns to the controller part), then the CSI node plugin formats it with a filesystem if needed and mounts it, and the container sees it at a path such as /var/lib/db. The controller-versus-node split matches the work: cloud API calls happen once, centrally, while formatting and mounting must happen on the specific host. Volume snapshots in Kubernetes also depend on CSI drivers.

quiz.q: What is the division of labor between a CSI driver's controller part and node part?
quiz.a: The controller calls the storage/cloud API to create, delete, attach and snapshot volumes; the node part formats and mounts the device on the host running the pod.

title: Kubernetes snapshots mirror the PV/PVC pattern
body: Kubernetes models volume snapshots with three objects. VolumeSnapshot is a user's request, like a PVC. VolumeSnapshotContent is the actual snapshot, like a PV. VolumeSnapshotClass holds driver parameters, like a StorageClass. They are custom resource definitions, work only with CSI drivers, and require a snapshot controller to be installed. Snapshots are crash-consistent by default. A new PVC can be created from a snapshot, or cloned directly from another existing PVC.
deeper: Mirroring the familiar PV/PVC/StorageClass trio makes snapshots easy to reason about: users ask for a snapshot without knowing how the backend takes it, and the driver produces an actual snapshot object bound to that request. Because the objects are CRDs rather than core built-in types, clusters need the snapshot CRDs and a snapshot controller installed, and the storage must use a CSI driver that supports snapshots; older in-tree plugins do not. Crash consistency carries over from the underlying cloud snapshot: the snapshot captures volume blocks at an instant, missing any data still in the page cache, and a restored database must replay its write-ahead log as after a crash. If you need application consistency, freeze the filesystem or have the database checkpoint before snapshotting, typically coordinated by an operator. Creating PVCs from snapshots or cloning PVCs enables useful workflows: restoring after a bad migration, standing up a copy of production data for testing, or seeding a new replica from existing data.

quiz.q: Which Kubernetes snapshot object plays the role of a PVC, and which plays the role of a PV?
quiz.a: VolumeSnapshot is the user's request, like a PVC; VolumeSnapshotContent is the actual snapshot, like a PV. VolumeSnapshotClass parallels a StorageClass.

title: StatefulSets: db-1 always comes back as db-1, with its disk
body: A StatefulSet runs pods that need stable identity. Each pod gets a stable name, such as db-0, db-1 and db-2, a stable network identity, and its own PVC created from a volumeClaimTemplate. If db-1 dies, its replacement is also named db-1 and reattaches the same PVC, so it finds its own data. Pods are created and updated in order. By default, deleting or scaling down a StatefulSet does not delete its PVCs, so data survives mistakes.
deeper: Stable identity is what distributed databases need. Replicas are not interchangeable: db-0 may be the primary, db-1 and db-2 replicas, each with its own copy of the data and a known address that peers and clients use. A regular Deployment would give replacements random names and no persistent per-pod storage, breaking those assumptions. The volumeClaimTemplate automatically creates a separate PVC per pod, such as one for db-0 and one for db-1, and binds each to the same-numbered pod forever. Ordered creation and updates matter for systems that must bootstrap in sequence or should only upgrade one member at a time. Keeping PVCs after deletion or scale-down is a safety choice: if someone accidentally scales from three to one, the data for db-1 and db-2 is still there when they scale back up. The limitation is important: StatefulSets manage identity and storage, not database logic. They cannot promote a replica, rebuild one or run backups, which is why operators exist.

quiz.q: If StatefulSet pod db-1 dies, what happens to its identity and data?
quiz.a: The replacement pod is also named db-1, keeps the same network identity and reattaches the same PVC, so it finds the same data.

title: What a StatefulSet does not do: it knows nothing about your database
body: A StatefulSet gives pods stable names and stable storage, but it knows nothing about the database running inside them. It will not promote a replica to primary when the primary fails. It will not rebuild a lost replica. It will not run backups. It will not perform a safe rolling upgrade that waits for replication to catch up before moving to the next pod. All of that database-specific operational knowledge must come from somewhere else, usually an operator.
deeper: This gap is where many teams underestimate the effort of running databases on Kubernetes. A StatefulSet's rolling update, for example, restarts pods in order, but it only knows whether a pod is running, not whether the replica inside has caught up with the primary. Restarting the next pod too early could leave the cluster with too few up-to-date copies. Similarly, if the primary pod's node dies, the StatefulSet will try to bring back the same-named pod with the same volume, which for a zonal or local volume may be slow or impossible, rather than promoting an existing replica. Backups, including consistency coordination such as checkpointing before snapshots, are simply outside its scope. These tasks are exactly what a human database administrator used to do, and on Kubernetes they must be automated for it to work well at scale. The chapter's next section introduces operators, controllers that encode that knowledge, and the senior staff lens asks whether the team has an operator it trusts and has practiced failures with.

quiz.q: Why is a StatefulSet's ordered rolling update not enough to safely upgrade a replicated database?
quiz.a: It only knows whether pods are running, not whether replication has caught up, so it may restart the next member before data is safely replicated.

title: Local persistent volumes: fast NVMe, pinned to one node
body: A local PersistentVolume exposes a node's local disk, for example NVMe flash, as a PV. It requires node affinity, so a pod using it can only run on that node. Local PVs do not support dynamic provisioning in core Kubernetes, and if the node fails, the pod cannot move elsewhere and the data may be lost. The Kubernetes docs recommend WaitForFirstConsumer binding for them. Local PVs make sense only when the application replicates its own data.
deeper: Local PVs bring the local-versus-network trade-off into Kubernetes. The benefit is local NVMe's performance: tens of microseconds of latency and very high IOPS, with no per-volume product caps. The costs are the same as outside Kubernetes but more visible. Node affinity pins the pod, so the scheduler loses its usual freedom; if the node dies or is replaced, the pod cannot be rescheduled with its data, and node replacement effectively means data loss for that replica. Without dynamic provisioning in core Kubernetes, local PVs must be pre-created or managed by additional tooling. WaitForFirstConsumer is recommended because the scheduler must weigh the pod's other constraints together with the location of available local disks before binding. The chapter explicitly ties this back to the rule from the local-versus-network section: use local storage only when the application replicates itself. The operational risk list adds that automation must detect a lost local replica and rebuild it, ideally within a computed, acceptable rebuild window.

quiz.q: When is a Kubernetes local PersistentVolume a reasonable choice for a database?
quiz.a: Only when the database replicates its own data, since the pod is pinned to one node and losing that node loses the replica's data.

title: Operators: putting the DBA's playbook into code
body: An operator is a Kubernetes controller that encodes operational knowledge for one specific system: how to bootstrap it, add a replica, fail over, back up and upgrade. It fills exactly the gap StatefulSets leave. Where a StatefulSet only keeps pods and volumes stable, an operator understands the database inside, so it can promote a replica when the primary dies, rebuild lost replicas, run backups and perform rolling upgrades that wait for replication health.
deeper: Operators follow the Kubernetes pattern of reconciling actual state toward desired state, but with domain logic. A database operator might watch a custom resource that declares 'a three-replica cluster, version X, daily backups', then continuously act to make that true: creating the StatefulSet, checking replication lag, failing over when the primary is unreachable, triggering snapshots after asking the database to checkpoint, and coordinating upgrades one member at a time. It also handles the Kubernetes-specific risks the chapter lists. During node drains, it should wait for replication health before allowing the next drain. If a volume detach is stuck, it should fail over to a replica rather than wait. With local PVs, it should detect a lost replica and rebuild it. In short, the operator is where the DBA's playbook lives as code. The quality of that code determines whether running databases on Kubernetes is safe, which is why the senior staff lens asks whether the team trusts its operator and has practiced failures with it.

quiz.q: What does an operator do that a StatefulSet does not?
quiz.a: It encodes system-specific operations: bootstrapping, promoting a replica on failure, rebuilding lost replicas, running backups and rolling upgrades that wait for replication health.

title: Rook: a CNCF-graduated operator that runs Ceph on Kubernetes
body: Rook is a CNCF graduated operator for Ceph, the open-source distributed storage system. It automates deploying, configuring, scaling, upgrading and monitoring Ceph clusters on Kubernetes. Through Ceph, it provides three kinds of storage to other pods: block storage via RBD, file storage via CephFS, and object storage via RGW. Rook's Ceph operator was declared stable in December 2018, making it a mature example of encoding a complex storage system's operations in software.
deeper: Rook shows operators managing not just a database but a whole storage platform. Ceph is powerful but operationally demanding: it has many daemons, placement rules, failure handling and upgrade procedures. Rook turns those procedures into automation, so a team can run Ceph as a set of Kubernetes resources and let the operator handle deployment, scaling and upgrades. Once running, Ceph becomes a storage provider for the rest of the cluster: pods can claim RBD block volumes much like cloud volumes, share CephFS filesystems for ReadWriteMany needs, or use RGW's object interface. Ceph's own CSI driver, mentioned among the examples of vendor drivers, connects those volumes to pods through the standard interface. This pattern suits organizations running Kubernetes on their own hardware, where no cloud block storage exists, letting them build a disaggregated storage pool from local disks across nodes. The December 2018 stability milestone gives a sense of how long the approach has been proven.

quiz.q: What three storage interfaces does Rook-managed Ceph provide to other pods?
quiz.a: Block storage via RBD, file storage via CephFS, and object storage via RGW.

title: HubSpot and Vitess: from first operator to 1,000+ MySQL clusters
body: Vitess, the MySQL sharding and management system, has a Kubernetes operator. HubSpot adopted Vitess on Kubernetes from mid-2016. A 2019 CNCF case study says HubSpot built the first Vitess operator and had run it in production for about two years, and its engineers said Vitess let them unify data storage and microservices infrastructure on Kubernetes. By 2023, HubSpot reported running over a thousand MySQL clusters per environment on Vitess.
deeper: HubSpot's story demonstrates that the operator pattern can carry serious relational workloads at scale. Before operators, companies typically ran databases on dedicated VMs managed by separate tooling, while applications ran on Kubernetes, creating two operational worlds. By building a Vitess operator, HubSpot put the operation of its Vitess-managed MySQL into Kubernetes automation, and its engineers said this let them unify data storage and microservices infrastructure on one platform. The scale is the notable part: by 2023 HubSpot reported over a thousand MySQL clusters per environment on Vitess, far beyond what manual administration could handle. It also fits the chapter's broader themes. Vitess replicates data at the database layer, which is what makes it compatible with application-managed durability, and PlanetScale later built Metal on Vitess with local NVMe. HubSpot's experience also answers the senior staff lens's key question: it had an operator it built and trusted, run in production for years.

quiz.q: What did HubSpot gain by running Vitess on Kubernetes with an operator?
quiz.a: Its engineers said it unified data storage and microservices infrastructure on Kubernetes, and it later grew to over a thousand MySQL clusters per environment on Vitess by 2023.

title: Stateful K8s risks: node drains and zonal volumes
body: Two failure modes hit databases on Kubernetes hard. First, node drains and upgrades: a cluster upgrade drains nodes one by one, and for a database each drain is a failover. Use PodDisruptionBudgets so no more than one replica is down at a time, and make the operator wait for replication health before the next drain. Second, zonal volumes: an EBS volume cannot move to another AZ, so if a zone fails, pods whose PVCs live there cannot reschedule elsewhere.
deeper: Drains are routine for stateless apps: pods get evicted and restart elsewhere in seconds with nothing lost. For a replicated database, evicting the primary triggers a failover, and evicting replicas reduces redundancy. If an upgrade drains nodes faster than replicas can resync, the cluster could end up with multiple members down or behind at once. A PodDisruptionBudget tells Kubernetes the minimum number of pods that must stay available, blocking voluntary evictions that would violate it, and the operator adds the database-aware check that a restarted replica has caught up before the next drain proceeds. Zonal volumes are a hard physical constraint. Because EBS replicates only inside one AZ and cannot move between zones, a zone outage strands every pod whose data lives there; Kubernetes can reschedule the pod, but not its volume. The only defense is application-level replication across zones, so replicas in surviving zones can take over. This echoes the earlier lesson that on AWS, cross-AZ durability is the application's job.

quiz.q: Why must database replicas on Kubernetes span zones at the application level when using EBS?
quiz.a: EBS volumes cannot move across AZs, so a zone failure strands pods whose PVCs live there. Only replicas in other zones can take over.

title: Stateful K8s risks: stuck detaches and lost local disks
body: Two more risks. Volume attach and detach delays: moving a network volume to a new node takes time, and a stuck detach, when the old node is unreachable, can block the new pod for minutes. Operators should fail over to a replica rather than wait for the volume. Local PV loss: with local disks, replacing a node means losing that replica's data. Automation must detect the loss and rebuild the replica from its peers, without waiting for a human.
deeper: A stuck detach happens because the storage system must be sure the old node is no longer writing before attaching the volume elsewhere; if the old node is unreachable rather than cleanly dead, the system may wait before forcing the detach. For a database primary, those minutes are an outage. The operator's better move is to promote an existing replica, whose data is already attached and up to date, and deal with the old volume later. This mirrors the recovery comparison from the local-versus-network section: reattaching a network volume is usually fast, but not always, so replicas remain the fastest failover path. Local PV loss is the other side of local storage: a node replacement during an upgrade, or a hardware failure, silently removes a replica's data. If automation does not notice, the cluster runs with reduced redundancy indefinitely. The rebuild itself takes time proportional to data size divided by allowed bandwidth, the calculation that showed about 2.2 hours for 10 TB throttled to 1.25 GB/s.

quiz.q: If a database primary's old node is unreachable and its volume detach is stuck, what should the operator do?
quiz.a: Fail over to an existing replica rather than wait minutes for the volume to detach and reattach to a new node.

title: Stateful K8s risks: deleted namespaces and noisy neighbor pods
body: The last two risks. Accidental deletion: a single kubectl delete namespace can remove PVCs, and with a Delete reclaim policy the cloud volumes go too, destroying the data. Defend with the Retain policy, deletion protection and off-cluster backups. Noisy neighbors: pods on the same node share the node's network bandwidth to EBS and the instance's EBS limits, so one heavy pod can slow others. Put heavy databases on dedicated node pools to isolate them.
deeper: Accidental deletion is dangerous because Kubernetes makes deletion cascade conveniently. Removing a namespace removes everything in it, including PVCs, and a Delete reclaim policy extends the cascade to the actual cloud disks. The layered defense matters: Retain stops the cascade at the volume, deletion protection guards the resources themselves, and off-cluster backups ensure recovery even if something inside the cluster or account is destroyed. Backups that live only in the same cluster can vanish in the same mistake. Noisy neighbors reappear at the node level even after EBS solved much of the problem at the storage layer. Each instance has limited bandwidth to EBS, and every pod on the node competes for it, so a batch job doing heavy I/O can inflate the database's latency. Dedicated node pools, groups of nodes reserved for database workloads, give heavy databases the instance's full EBS bandwidth and predictable performance. Both risks are examples of the general point that stateful workloads need different guardrails than stateless apps.

quiz.q: Why are off-cluster backups needed even with a Retain reclaim policy?
quiz.a: Retain protects only against PVC deletion cascading to volumes. Backups outside the cluster survive broader mistakes or losses that could destroy in-cluster data.

title: Senior staff lens: can your operator fail over under real failure?
body: The real question is not 'can Kubernetes run databases?' It can. The question is whether the team has an operator it trusts to fail over, rebuild and upgrade, and whether it has practiced those operations under real failure. Many companies choose managed databases or dedicated VMs for their largest stores, and use Kubernetes for the long tail of smaller databases, where standard automation matters more than squeezing out every bit of latency.
deeper: This lens reframes a common debate into something testable. Kubernetes provides the building blocks, PVCs, StorageClasses, CSI, StatefulSets, but the safety of a database on it rests almost entirely on the operator's behavior during bad moments: a node drained mid-upgrade, a stuck volume detach, a lost local disk, a zone outage. An operator that has never been exercised under those conditions is an untested disaster-recovery plan. Practicing means deliberately injecting failures and verifying that failover, rebuild and upgrade behave as expected. The split strategy many companies adopt follows from economics. The largest, most performance-critical stores justify dedicated infrastructure or a managed service, where latency can be tuned carefully and specialists focus on a few systems. The long tail, hundreds or thousands of smaller databases, benefits most from Kubernetes' standardized automation, since manual care per database is impossible at that count. HubSpot, with over a thousand MySQL clusters per environment on Vitess by 2023 after building its own Vitess operator, shows how far that kind of standard automation can scale.

quiz.q: Why do many companies run only their long tail of databases on Kubernetes, not their largest stores?
quiz.a: For many small databases, standard automation matters most. The largest stores need tuned latency and specialist care, often via managed databases or dedicated VMs.

title: EFS, Filestore, Azure Files: shared POSIX filesystems as a service
body: Sometimes many machines need to share the same POSIX filesystem, for example shared home directories, content management, ML notebooks and legacy apps. Clouds offer managed network filesystems. Amazon EFS uses NFSv4.1, with elastic capacity and data stored across multiple AZs in its regional classes. Google Filestore is managed NFS for Compute Engine and GKE. Azure Files provides managed SMB and NFS shares. These are the usual backing for Kubernetes ReadWriteMany volumes.
deeper: Block storage and object storage do not cover this need. A block volume normally attaches to one machine at a time, because a block device has no coordination between writers, and object storage lacks POSIX semantics such as in-place edits, directories and file locking that legacy software expects. Network filesystems fill the gap by letting many clients mount the same tree and see each other's changes through standard file APIs. EFS stands out for durability: its regional classes store data across multiple Availability Zones, unlike single-AZ EBS, and its capacity grows automatically without provisioning. Filestore integrates with Google's VMs and Kubernetes; Azure Files supports both SMB, common for Windows workloads, and NFS. In Kubernetes, a ReadWriteMany claim, one mountable read-write by many nodes, is typically satisfied by one of these services, which is why they appear in shared-content and notebook platforms. The trade-off, covered next, is performance on metadata-heavy operations, which limits where these filesystems belong.

quiz.q: Why do Kubernetes ReadWriteMany volumes usually rely on services like EFS rather than block volumes?
quiz.a: Block volumes typically attach to one node with no cross-writer coordination; managed network filesystems provide shared POSIX access for many clients simultaneously.

title: Shared filesystems: great for sharing, bad for databases
body: Managed network filesystems are convenient, but keeping POSIX semantics consistent across many clients makes metadata operations, such as open, stat and creating small files, much slower than on a local disk. That makes them a poor fit for databases and for workloads with millions of tiny files. The chapter's guidance is clear: large-scale analytics should use object storage instead, and databases should use block storage. Shared filesystems belong to genuinely shared-file use cases.
deeper: The cost comes from coordination. On a local disk, opening or statting a file is a quick in-kernel operation. On a network filesystem, the server must keep every client's view consistent, so metadata operations often require network round trips and server-side coordination, adding latency to each one. A workload that touches millions of small files multiplies that latency millions of times. Databases suffer for related reasons: they need fast, predictable random I/O and reliable fsync semantics, and a shared filesystem adds network and protocol overhead with none of the benefits, since only one database instance should write its files anyway. Analytics over huge datasets benefits more from object storage, which scales throughput massively and avoids POSIX metadata costs. The resulting map summarizes much of the book so far: objects for immutable bulk data and analytics, block volumes, network or local, for databases, and shared filesystems only when multiple machines truly need the same POSIX tree, such as home directories, notebooks or legacy applications.

quiz.q: Why are shared network filesystems a poor fit for workloads with millions of tiny files?
quiz.a: POSIX consistency across clients makes metadata operations like open, stat and small-file creates much slower than local disk, and that cost multiplies per file.

title: Kafka skips fsync, PostgreSQL panics on it: both are right
body: Kafka's documentation says durability does not require fsync, while PostgreSQL treats an fsync failure as fatal. Both are correct because durability lives in different layers. Kafka relies on replication: a failed broker recovers its data from other replicas, so local fsync is not the source of durability. PostgreSQL relies on its local write-ahead log being on disk for committed transactions, and after an fsync error the kernel may have dropped dirty pages, so the only safe action is to crash and recover.
deeper: This pairing ties together the chapter's central themes. First, where durability lives: Kafka puts it in the replication layer, PostgreSQL puts it in the local storage layer, and each design follows consistently from that choice. The senior staff advice to put durability in exactly one layer, on purpose, is visible here. Second, storage choice: because Kafka's durability does not depend on any one disk, it fits local NVMe well; a single-node PostgreSQL without replicas needs durable network volumes and snapshots, while a replicated setup might go local, as PlanetScale did with Vitess-managed MySQL. Third, the fsync mechanics: write() only reaches the page cache; fsync forces data to stable storage; commit rate is bounded by fsync latency; and on Linux a failed write-back can mark pages clean and drop data, so a retried fsync may falsely succeed. The key takeaways compress it into one line: databases live or die by fsync, and an fsync error means the page cache cannot be trusted.

quiz.q: Why does Kafka say durability doesn't require fsync, while PostgreSQL treats fsync failure as fatal?
quiz.a: Kafka's durability comes from replicas on other brokers. PostgreSQL depends on its local WAL being on disk, and after an fsync error dropped pages make crash-and-replay the only safe path.
